newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Summit torn by disputes over European security.
newsitem.headline: Summit torn by disputes over European security.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
Russia attacked NATO's plans for enlargement and Belarus came under fire at a security summit on Monday, sounding a jarring note as some 50 nations promised to build a lasting peace in Europe.

The first day of the summit was also marked by a fierce dispute between Armenia and Azerbaijan which threatened to block the entire summit declaration, and by growing concern over Serbia's handling of mass protests on the streets of Belgrade.

Leaders from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) did manage to agree on a new round of arms control talks that would adapt and extend a Cold War-era agreement cutting conventional force in Europe.
They also agreed on a security blueprint for the 21st century, a set of concepts designed to make all nations feel secure on the continent where two world wars have started.

But the veneer of diplomatic harmony was shattered almost from the start, when Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told assembled leaders that NATO would create new fault lines in Europe if it went ahead with plans to take in countries from Eastern Europe as new members.
"Is it not clear that the appearance of new dividing lines would lead to a worsening of the whole geopolitical situation in the world?" Chernomyrdin asked the opening session of the two-day meeting.
The last summit of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), two years ago in Budapest, was wrecked by a row on the NATO issue and differences over Bosnia.
The United States and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana insisted that the alliance posed no threat to anyone and that it wanted to cooperate with Russia.

"NATO has been and remains a defensive alliance...it poses no threat to any other state," U.S. Vice President Al Gore told the summit. "The stability that NATO can help extend to Central Europe can help ensure the security of all nations."
Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus told reporters his country still expected to be among the first to join the alliance, and Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said:
"Moscow has trouble accepting that NATO's enlargement is a foregone conclusion."

However, the Lisbon meeting did reach agreement on an issue of concern to Russia -- adapting and extending a 1990 arms treaty which Moscow says no longer reflects reality. A new round of negotiations is now expected to start in Vienna in January.
Western nations told Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, accused of trying to acquire dictatorial powers, to put the former Soviet republic back on the track to democracy.
A defiant Lukashenko responded by supporting Russia's opposition to NATO expansion, denying there was any problem at home and telling leaders to mind their own business.
"It would be counterproductive to try to exert pressure on us or try to interfere in our internal affairs," he said.

The summit is expected to endorse a continued OSCE role in Bosnia, one year after the war ended there, although most eyes were on Serbia and the unprecedented challenge from demonstrators to President Slobodan Milosevic's autocratic rule.
International peace coordinator Carl Bildt called for Milosevic to start radical democratic reforms and to drop a threat to crush the protests.

A senior U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, said there could not be a "decent peace in the Balkans" unless Serbia became an open society, while British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind also called for greater democracy there.
Russia has won little support at the summit for its proposals to give the OSCE a more powerful role in European security and have it act as a counterbalance to NATO.

France and Germany showed some sympathy for Russian concerns, but many other countries fear Moscow wants to gain an effective veto on important European security issues by changing the way the OSCE works.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told the meeting Europe must not miss the chance to build real cooperation.
"There can only be security in Europe with, not against, Russia," the German leader said.
The security blueprint adopted by the summit reflects such differences, balancing Russian concerns with the desires of NATO allies and Eastern European nations to press on with expansion.
It said countries would consider developing a charter on European security, something Moscow wants, but reaffirmed the rights of all nations to join alliances.

Diplomats said the row between Armenia and Azerbaijan over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh could torpedo the final summit communique, which was due to be issued on Tuesday. Every country in the OSCE has a veto.
